title: The id you can change
brief: 17:20. The mobile app calls the orders API. A partner reports that changing one number in a request returned somebody else's order.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The API checks that the caller has a valid token, and never that the order is theirs.
teaches: Every endpoint that takes an object id must check the caller may access that object
Scope the data access itself, and test other people's ids in CI
Random ids and hidden fields are not authorization

value.title: Orders API

lines: Auth: bearer token, one per customer account.
Orders belong to a customer: order.customerId.

value.intro: You hold a valid token for customer 88, who owns order 1002. Ask for your order, then for the next number along.

attempts.label: GET order 1003
Loop over 1000 to 1500
attempts.response:
501 requests, 501 x HTTP 200.
Every order in the range was returned: 47 customers' details.

fix.step: Pick the fix that closes the hole
fix.prompt: Pick every change that makes the API check ownership of the object, and keeps it checked as the API grows.

options.label: Scope the data access to the caller: look up by id and customer
code: + const order = await Orders.findOne({ id: req.params.id, customerId: req.auth.customerId });
options.why: The API only returns an object that belongs to the caller. Return not found for everything else so ids cannot be probed.

options.label: Add a test that requests another customer's object and expects not found
code: + test('customer 88 cannot read order 1003', async () => expect(await get('/v1/orders/1003', as(88))).toBe(404));
options.why: The check becomes part of the build, so the next endpoint cannot quietly skip it.

options.label: Switch to random UUIDs for order ids
options.why: Harder to guess, but ids leak in emails, logs and shared links, and whoever holds one can read the order.

options.label: Only check that the token is valid, and that the caller has the customer role
options.why: Every customer has that role, so it lets everyone in. The question is not what the caller is, but whose object this is.

options.label: Rate limit the orders endpoint
options.why: Slows scraping, but one request is enough to read someone's order.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.insight: The API checks that the caller has a valid token, and never that the order is theirs.

Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The API authenticated the caller and then returned whatever object the id named. Order 1003 belongs to another customer and came back complete, and a loop returned 47 customers' details in seconds.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: A valid token, someone else's order
body: The API authenticated the caller and then returned whatever object the id named. Order 1003 belongs to another customer and came back complete, and a loop returned 47 customers' details in seconds.
This is number one on the API list because it is the easiest thing to forget.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Untick this one, it does not fix the cause
Pick this change
Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Scoping the lookup by customer means the data layer only ever returns the caller's own objects. The test turns “someone else's id” into a build failure, so the next endpoint cannot skip the check.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: The object belongs to the caller, or it does not exist
body: Scoping the lookup by customer means the data layer only ever returns the caller's own objects. The test turns “someone else's id” into a build failure, so the next endpoint cannot skip the check.
Check the object, not just the caller.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: UUIDs make ids hard to guess, but any id that ever leaks is still readable by anyone, because the server still does not check ownership. A role check lets every customer in, since they all have the role.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Guessing was never the problem
body: UUIDs make ids hard to guess, but any id that ever leaks is still readable by anyone, because the server still does not check ownership. A role check lets every customer in, since they all have the role.
Ownership of the object is the check.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
